86.s: Edison names Columbus figures like Joe Thomas and Sy Oliver and trombonist Archie Hall and Paul Tyler, who stayed home.
86.q: Columbus? There was Joe Thomas who played with Jimmie Lunceford, he was from Columbus, OH. Sy Oliver, he stayed around Columbus, OH for years but his home was right outside of Columbus, OH. Not Youngstown, that’s too far. But he’s a Buckeye—everybody from Ohio they’re called Buckeyes—but he stayed…

86.t: Back in Columbus: Pete France and local bandsmen
86.s: His mother brought him to Columbus; he names Pete France, Paul Tyler, Sy Oliver, Jimmy Crawford and Zack White's band.
86.q: Oh, yes, when I got 12 years old she came and took me back to Columbus, Ohio. And there was a fantastic trumpet player at the time, a great friend of Sy Oliver's. He had a band around there named Pete France. Pete France, yes. Great man. He had a band around Columbus, Ohio. I'll tell you who was…

86.t: Columbus musicians: Earl Hood, John Hooks, Paul Tyler
86.s: Edison lists good local players and bands.
86.q: And they had some pretty good musicians in Columbus. Had a trombone player there, his name was Archie -- oh, he played with Jim Europe's band years ago.* Fantastic trombone player. And they had a band around there that was called Earl Hood's band, Hooks, trumpet player, John Hooks. He was from…

86.t: Ohio as a center for bands and musicians
86.s: He names musicians from Ohio and explains how Columbus sat near Cincinnati, Cleveland and other dance towns.
86.q: He's from Zanesville. And the Mills Brothers are from Pickaway, Ohio. They're from Ohio. Earl Warren is from Ohio. Teddy Wilson spent a lot of time in Ohio with Speed Webb, he was from Ohio. Chick Carter, Snooky Young's old boss, he's from Ohio. Art Tatum was from Toledo. There are many, many good…

107.t: Collegians personnel: Jimmy Wilkins, H. D. Whalem and Freeman Lee
107.s: An 18-piece dance band led by veteran Jimmy Wilkins; Foster describes Whalem, and trumpeter Freeman Lee, who later recorded with him and Elmo Hope.
107.q: The Collegians were about 18 pieces, a full-sized dance band. We played for college dances. We traveled to places as far away as Knoxville, Kentucky, and Indianapolis, Indiana.

107.t: What became of the Collegians' players
107.s: Foster recalls Whalem, Lee, Jimmy Wilkins, Clarence Johnson, Reynauld Davis, Rufus Bond, James Warren and the two-drummer, two-bass setup; he left before his senior year.
107.q: Yeah. The Collegians were a popular group on campus. I wasn’t the most popular of the Collegians. The most popular was the guy I referred to as H. D. Whalem, who played tenor, trumpet, and sang. He was short in stature, so they called him “Peanut.” He was probably more popular even for that fact.…

70.t: Bob Carroll and the musicians from Louisville and the Midwest
70.s: Bob Carroll, Dickie Wells, Frankie Newton, Bill Coleman, Jonah Jones and Buddy Lee came out of Louisville; Ohio, Indiana and Illinois had many territory bands.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Bob Carroll, he was from Louisville, like a lot of good musicians came out of Louisville. Dickie Wells came out of Louisville. I think Frankie Newton came out of Louisville. I think Bill Coleman, too.

70.t: Al Sears and Buffalo as a center for musicians
70.s: Al Sears came from Zanesville and played with Zack White in 1929; Buffalo hosted Alphonso Trent, Lunceford and Stuff Smith.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: And he played with Zack Whyte before I joined the band. He played with Zack Whyte in '29. He played baritone, you know. He used to stomp his foot way high to get that rhythm, you know. He left there and went to Buffalo, like a lot of musicians.

144.t: Ohio, Cleveland tenor players and Buffalo vocal groups
144.s: Fuller recalls Mel Wanzo in Ohio, a Cleveland tenor called Joe, Grant Green and the Burrell family, and Hendricks's brother's group in Buffalo.
144.q: He was the cat. He was a big guy. He looked like George Colon. I can’t think of his name. Then there was another guy they called Popeye. He had another name. He did some dates around with some good people. He was still lingering with the other stuff.

112.t: Detroit's big bands and the Dixieland repertoire
112.s: Detroit had twelve-piece bands led by men like Bart Howard, while Wooding's combination played Margie and St. Louis Blues.
112.ch: Philadelphia, Detroit and back to Atlantic City
112.q: Well, they had four or five great bands. One fellow that had a great band was named Bart Howard. Now, they had large bands there. They had bands of 12 pieces, and like that. I don't think there was any larger than
